articles.title: Supplements: what do athletes take and why?
articles.summary: There is a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in the pursuit of marginal gains - what do they take and why?
articles.body:
It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.

Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance â a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.

Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.

But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' â even if it was legal.

From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.

Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.

"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.

"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."

So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?

While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.

Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.

"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.

Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.

Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.

During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 â effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".

In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.

According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".

The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (Â£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (Â£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research. , external

Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.

"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.

"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.

"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."

Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.

"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.

"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating â all of those things â before we add in all of the extras."

Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.

Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.

Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.

"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.

"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.

"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."

Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.

So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?

"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.

"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.

"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."

But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.

"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.

And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.

There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.

One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.

While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.

If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.

In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.

"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.

Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".

There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."

He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.

"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.

There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge â and some are going back to basics.

For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative â from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.

It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.

The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.

Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.

In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.

These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.

British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.

"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."

As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.

She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."

Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.

"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."

She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".

"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."

"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.

"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

articles.title: St Helens appoint Australia boss Kevin Walters as head coach for next three Super League seasons
articles.summary: Kevin Walters has signed a three-year deal with St Helens to take the reins at the club; He is currently the Australia head coach and will lead them at this autumn's World Cup; round 24 of Super League continues on Thursday August 20, live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
St Helens have announced the appointment of Australia boss Kevin Walters as their head coach on a three-year deal from the start of the 2027 Super League season.

As the Kangaroos' head coach, Walters guided Australia to a 3-0 whitewash over England in last autumn's Ashes series.

Prior to taking on the international role, Walters was in charge of Brisbane Broncos, whom he guided to the NRL Grand Final in 2023.

  • Super League's Final Charge: Seven teams in contention
  • Super League fixtures & results | Super League table
  • Get Sky Sports or stream contract-free on NOW
  • Choose the Sky Sports notifications you want

He has also taking charge of Queensland and had a prior brief stint in Super League in 2009 and 2010 with Catalans Dragons.

Walters will take the reins at the Saints following the conclusion of the Rugby League World Cup this autumn.

Reports in Australia suggest that it is the biggest coaching deal offered in St Helens' 153-year history.

St Helens sacked head coach Paul Rowley just 17 games into his time at the club amid a difficult 2026 season and assistant coach Eamonn O'Carroll has been in charge since as the club battle to try and not miss the play-offs for the first time in their history.

On joining St Helens, Walters said: "St Helens are one of the most iconic and successful brands in rugby league. I am honoured to be given the opportunity by the Chairman, Eamonn McManus, and the St Helens Board to lead a club with so much history.

"I look forward to bringing my experiences as a Coach and blending those learnings into the winning culture of St Helens.

"For me, the foundation of success is creating the right environment where the players and staff enjoy coming to training and working hard for each other, as well as the Saints sponsors, fans and the wider community.

"At the end of last year, I was in England for the Ashes Series as the Kangaroos Head Coach. I witnessed first-hand how tough, physical, and skilful the English players were. I look forward to being a part of Super League in 2027 with the Saints."

Chairman Eamonn McManus added: "Kevin's vast experience at both club and representative levels is self-evident.

"His motivation to succeed with the task at hand was both clear and compelling to us, as shown by the major career sacrifices that he is making in Australia to join St Helens.

"This is a major statement of ambition both by St.Helens and by Super League.

"We would like to place on record our thanks to the understanding and professionalism of Peter V'Landys and the ARL Commission in facilitating Kevin's move to us.

"Eamon O'Carroll will continue as our interim head coach until the end of this season. He has been magnificent for us under testing circumstances, and I am sure that our fans will remain firmly behind him and the team."

Reports in Australia suggest that it is the biggest coaching deal offered in St Helens' 153-year history.

St Helens sacked head coach Paul Rowley just 17 games into his time at the club amid a difficult 2026 season and assistant coach Eamonn O'Carroll has been in charge since as the club battle to try and not miss the play-offs for the first time in their history.

On joining St Helens, Walters said: "St Helens are one of the most iconic and successful brands in rugby league. I am honoured to be given the opportunity by the Chairman, Eamonn McManus, and the St Helens Board to lead a club with so much history.

"I look forward to bringing my experiences as a Coach and blending those learnings into the winning culture of St Helens.

"For me, the foundation of success is creating the right environment where the players and staff enjoy coming to training and working hard for each other, as well as the Saints sponsors, fans and the wider community.

"At the end of last year, I was in England for the Ashes Series as the Kangaroos Head Coach. I witnessed first-hand how tough, physical, and skilful the English players were. I look forward to being a part of Super League in 2027 with the Saints."

Chairman Eamonn McManus added: "Kevin's vast experience at both club and representative levels is self-evident.

"His motivation to succeed with the task at hand was both clear and compelling to us, as shown by the major career sacrifices that he is making in Australia to join St Helens.

"This is a major statement of ambition both by St.Helens and by Super League.

"We would like to place on record our thanks to the understanding and professionalism of Peter V'Landys and the ARL Commission in facilitating Kevin's move to us.

"Eamon O'Carroll will continue as our interim head coach until the end of this season. He has been magnificent for us under testing circumstances, and I am sure that our fans will remain firmly behind him and the team."

articles.title: Mikey Lewis: Hull KR playmaker banned for two matches for dangerous contact with Warrington Wolves' Ewan Irwin
articles.summary: Mikey Lewis has received a two-match ban for dangerous contact which will see him miss Rounds 25 and 26 of Super League; he had just returned from a four-match ban for a headbutt; round 24 of Super League commences from Thursday August 20, live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Hull KR's Mikey Lewis has been banned for two matches for dangerous contact with Warrington Wolves' Ewan Irwin during their rearranged round two Super League match on Tuesday night.

Lewis was sent to the sin bin when his studs hit Irwin's ankle as he sent up a kick, and he has been given a Grade C charge.

The ban will take effect from Round 25 which means he can play against Toulouse on Saturday but then will miss games against Wigan Warriors and Huddersfield Giants.

That would mean he returns for the final round of the regular season.

It is not known yet if the Robins will appeal the ban.

Lewis had just returned from a four-match ban which he copped for a headbutt the last time Hull KR played Warrington.

During that period, his side won all four matches without their star half-back.

It was wondered whether Hull KR would stick with Ryan Hampshire due to their winning run, but Peters opted to bring Lewis back in, citing the learning curve he has been on over the last month.

However, Peters faces a conundrum that Lewis is available for just two of their four remaining matches until the play-offs.

At the time, Warrington Wolves head coach Sam Burgess referred to the contact as "very dangerous" while Peters said he did not feel there was any "intent" behind the action.

Hull KR's Tevita Pangai Jr has also received a four-match ban, which means he would not be available until the semi-finals, if Peters' side were to make it that far.

He was cited for 'late contact on a passer' in three instances, two charged as Grade A and one as Grade B.

Due to already having a hefty amount of points on his record due to an eye gouge on Leeds Rhinos' Jake Connor earlier in the season, he could potentially not play in a Rovers shirt again.

Sky Sports will show every game of the Super League live this season, including two matches each round exclusively live. The remaining five matches will be broadcast on Sky Sports+.

articles.title: 6 NHL Free-Agent Landing Spots for Vladimir Tarasenko Amid Rumors
articles.summary: With NHL training camp approaching, there are a few big-name players still looking for a place to play and Vladimir Tarasenko might be the most accomplished among them.
articles.body:
With NHL training camp approaching, there are a few big-name players still looking for a place to play and Vladimir Tarasenko might be the most accomplished among them.

The 34-year-old sniper had a bounce-back season with Minnesota last year after a disappointing campaign in Detroit the previous year. In 75 games, he had 23 goals and 24 assists for 47 points.

He had five goals and eight assists on the power play, and if there's a good way to market him to a team in need, it's his ability to help on the man advantage.

Surely there's a market for a player who can still produce offensively and brings Stanley Cup-winning experience? If his defensive effort were stronger, we might not be writing about him.

That said, anyone who can chip in close to 50 points in a season should have a market and we've picked out some teams who could definitely make use of Tarasenko's skills.

When it came to scoring last season, the Flames were not associated with that in any way. Calgary scored the fewest goals in the NHL (208) and had the league's second-worst power play (16.2 percent).

With that lack of offensive output, how could the Flames not be interested in Vladimir Tarasenko?

He would have been Calgary's leading scorer with his output last season. He scored more goals (23) than any other Flames player. Even though his season was solid, it wasn't the best of his career, yet it was still better than anyone else on the Calgary roster.

The case for adding Tarasenko is easy because he would help the Flames score more goals and potentially win more games. His defensive play might not always be up to snuff, but it was an offensive desert in Calgary last season.

And if Tarasenko plays well and the Flames aren't in the playoff race, it would be an opportunity for Calgary to move him to a contender.

Chicago had a bold offseason, bringing back Patrick Kane and adding Bowen Byram to the defense. With how poor their offense was last season, those two will help give them a lift.

But with so many young players figuring out their games in the NHL, adding Vladimir Tarasenko to the mix could give the Blackhawks a bit of insurance in case they can't.

Chicago is well-acquainted with Tarasenko after his many seasons with the St. Louis Blues and again last season in Minnesota. It knows about his shot, how he works on the power play and how he would fit into its lineup.

Although you could argue that bringing Kane back fills that need, you could also suggest Chicago just needs more, especially with Connor Bedard likely missing the start of the season.

Tarasenko and his goal-scoring could give the Blackhawks a boost when times get tough for their younger players.

This offseason has been fascinating for Edmonton following the arrival of new head coach Mike Babcock, but they're also a team looking to get back to the Stanley Cup Final.

They're not hurting for offense with Connor McDavid and Leon Draisaitl, but bringing in an experienced shooter like Vladimir Tarasenko could give them the cover they need for younger players.

While the Oilers are a team that may not need more firepower, they are looking at potentially throwing rookie Isaac Howard back into the fire again this season.

Although the 22-year-old struggled in the NHL last year, he had a solid AHL season. But with a new coach and the same high expectations, supporting him with a veteran like Tarasenko could be the kind of depth Edmonton is looking for.

Adding Tarasenko to an already outstanding Oilers power play would be a case of the rich getting richer, but more scoring depth for Edmonton at 5-on-5 would be a good thing.

The Flyers' boldness this summer in trying to land Leo Carlsson puts them firmly on any list for available scoring talent, and Vladimir Tarasenko more than fits that bill.

His scoring skill and great work on the power play would give Philly at least one ace in the hole and it would also give fellow Russian, Matvei Michkov, someone to learn from.

The Flyers had the NHL's worst power play last season (15.7 percent) and while they want their current players to get better at it, adding a shooter and playmaker like Tarasenko could give their man advantage some needed juice.

If there's a catch with adding Tarasenko, how coach Rick Tocchet would handle the player's more offense-minded style of play would be worth keeping an eye on.

Part of Toronto's offseason makeover under new GM John Chayka involved basically rebuilding the entire third and fourth lines.

While that's good for toughening up the defense, it may leave the Maple Leafs' offense relying too heavily on their star players to do all the scoring.

Adding Vladimir Tarasenko as an option on the cheap could give them the scoring depth to help buoy them.

His talent offensively is still strong, as he demonstrated last season in Minnesota.

The Leafs have Auston Matthews, William Nylander and John Tavares to lead the offense and adding Gavin McKenna in the draft should help them score more, but you can't help but look at the Toronto roster and think it needs more.

Tarasenko has some limitations defensively, but new coach Jim Hiller's system should help to that end.

The Canucks were the NHL's worst team last season for many reasons, but a big one was that they just didn't score enough goals.

That issue doesn't seem set to resolve itself heading into the new year, as they're lacking depth in a big way, which should put Vladimir Tarasenko on their radar.

His 23 goals would have tied him for the team lead with Jake DeBrusk, and his 47 points would have been the fourth-most on the squad. Although he wouldn't solve Vancouver's problems, he would help address them by adding another guy who can contribute to the offense.

If there's a catch here, it's that Tarasenko might not want to join a team that is unlikely to be a playoff contender, never mind a Stanley Cup hopeful. However, this could be a situation where he can play himself into a contender by the deadline if he shows out. It may not be the most ideal way to go about it, but it's an option.

articles.title: Jets' Woody Johnson Buys Stake in Aston Martin Aramco F1 Team
articles.summary: New York Jets owner Woody Johnson is entering a new business endeavor.
articles.body:
New York Jets owner Woody Johnson is entering a new business endeavor.

According to Jack Bell of NYJets.com, Johnson has acquired a stake in Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Team. He will also join Aston Martin's board of directors as the vice chairman.

Johnson, the former US Ambassador to the United Kingdom, said his experience led to a "deep appreciation" for the car brand.

"During my time as US Ambassador to the United Kingdom, I have developed a deep appreciation for Aston Martin's rich history, as well as Lawrence Stroll's [the Aston owner] strategic vision and entrepreneurial spirit," Johnson said in the official Aston Martin announcement.

"I am excited to partner with him and contribute to the continued development of the team, with the ambition of building an organization capable of competing at the very highest level of the sport. We also share a commitment to growing the fanbase in the United States and introducing even more fans to the excitement of Formula 1."

According to ESPN's Rich Cimini , Johnson will handle the team's commercial growth, with a focus on the United States. He won't be involved in any day-to-day management duties.

Johnson has owned the Jets since 2000, when he purchased them for $635 million. He also purchased a 43 percent stake in Crystal Palace of the English Premier League in 2025 for $254 million, per Cimini.

Johnson said in a statement that he aims to partner with Stroll with "ambition of building an organization capable of competing at the very highest level of the sport" and wants to continue growing the sport of F1 in the United States.

Johnson and the Jets are well known across the pond, as the team holds international marketing rights for the United Kingdom and Ireland as part of the NFL's Global Markets Program. New York has played four regular-season games in London.

While Johnson will have an eye on his new Formula 1 team, he'll keep his focus on trying to get the Jets back to relevancy. The team is in a 15-year playoff drought and figures to be in for another tough year in 2026.

articles.title: Meet teen superstar Yan Diomandé, the most expensive African soccer player in history
articles.summary: Yan Diomandé is set to have an incredibly bright future. At just 19, the attacker has signed for arguably the world’s biggest soccer team in Real Madrid and will begin his debut season for Los Blancos as they face Espanyol on Saturday.
articles.body: Yan Diomandé is set to have an incredibly bright future. At just 19, the attacker has signed for arguably the world’s biggest soccer team in Real Madrid and will begin his debut season for Los Blancos as they face Espanyol on Saturday. The Spanish giant signed the Ivory Coast international on a seven-year deal this summer, for a reported fee of $144.3 million. That not only makes him the most expensive African player in history, but one of the biggest transfers in all of soccer. But while many wax lyrical about his rags-to-riches story – one that saw him hone his skills in the United States – his is also a story of heartbreak and a reminder of the traps that lie in wait for young stars who aspire to become professionals. Diomandé was born in the city of Abidjan in the Ivory Coast. It was a humble childhood but one grounded by the importance of family and friends. A passion for soccer was there from the start and a young Diomandé could be found running on dirt pitches in just a pair of white sandals. In a letter he recently wrote for The Player’s Tribune, Diomandé says he was nicknamed after Brazilian legend Roberto Carlos because of his ability to strike the ball so hard. He was only getting started, but people could already see the natural ability that the youngster believed would one day take him to the top. He started playing more seriously for a local team where he saw his aspirations grow. It wasn’t long before he was telling friends he’d be the next Cristiano Ronaldo. The pivotal moment in that becoming a reality came when he was just 15. After representing his country at an under-17 tournament in Ghana, he caught the attention of scouts from around the world. All of a sudden, he was a boy in demand. But as is the case for a lot of young talent in the soccer industry, the teenager quickly became a commodity. Agents, coaches and teams all wanted to represent him, to sign him, to have some say in his future. Moving to Florida Eventually, through a convoluted arrangement of partnerships which stretched from Africa to the United States, Diomandé was offered the chance to join the DME Academy in Daytona Beach, Florida. He was just 15 at the time, but the move was supposed to help him develop in a professional environment which would prepare him for a life playing in the top echelons of the game. In truth, though, it was also a way of hiding him away from other agencies and teams that were sniffing around the player. The idea was that he would stay in the US until he was old enough to sign a professional contract at 18, per FIFA guidelines. So, with just a suitcase and a dream, Diomandé left his home and family in Africa on a one-way journey to the US. Picking him up from the airport in Miami was DME Academy’s director of soccer Todd Eason, a man who would become a father figure for a boy being pulled in every which direction. “Because he only spoke French, our communication was very limited on our drive back from Miami, which was four hours away,” the now Miami FC General Manager told CNN Sports over the phone. “We just exchanged little messages on Google Translate to try to get to know each other. But I also had other French-speaking players on the team, so it was kind of let me just hurry back to campus, let me introduce him to others that speak the language and try to get him comfortable there.” At DME, a small team of players would train up to six times a week and balance that with their studies. It allowed Diomandé to learn English and get used to a very different way of life. He quickly formed bonds within the team and, despite staying relatively quiet, would come alive on the pitch. He surprised even Eason, who had only watched his video highlights until then. Diomandé was not just faster than everyone else, he was more intelligent on the ball and was already confident leading by example. “I assumed we just had another strong player, maybe a little sharper than some of the other players that we had,” he said. “But I think once he touched the pitch and started playing, it was like, ‘Wait a minute.’ “Once I saw him, it was like, ‘Man, this is a different level than what I have and this is going to be fun.’ “To watch Diomandé play, it was just different in every way. I was very excited to have that opportunity and for the boys around him to be able to play with him because it was a considerable difference from the others.” Finding a new family Under Eason’s tutelage, Diomandé continued to develop not only as a player but as a person. But being away from his family wasn’t easy, especially in an industry that sometimes treats young players as cash cows. Instead of speaking only about the Beautiful Game, Eason would talk to Diomandé about his mother, who suffers from long-term health issues, and genuinely cared about the person behind the player. “He always wanted to get to the point where he could provide for his family and get his mom into hospitals to treat her,” Eason said. “I don’t think he’s driven by winning the Champions League; that’s a bonus, but he just wants to be playing at the highest level to be able to provide for his family and his friends.” Diomandé’s time at DME Academy ended in 2024, but he had already been invited to trials at professional clubs around the world. For several reasons, each would end up unsuccessful until a familiar agency got back involved. Ever since Diomandé had impressed scouts in Africa, he was being closely tracked and guided by American sports organization Blue Crow, which had invested in several professional teams across Europe. One of those teams at the time was Club Deportivo Leganés, which played in Spain’s top division, La Liga, at the time. With a keen interest in the African market, the club was tipped off about Diomandé at an early age and followed his progress in the US, eventually signing him in November 2024. The move was managed by Blue Crow, which was keen to secure its financial interest in Diomandé amid all the rising interest. The teenager’s move to Spain initially saw him play in the Leganés academy, then the reserves and then quickly rise through the ranks to the first team. Turning professional The club’s general manager Martín Ortega still remembers watching Diomandé train for the first time with the senior squad. “He was the best,” Ortega told CNN Sports. “The first time he took the ball, it felt like you were watching something special. You know, it was something impressive, special, not common at all. “Even some of the players of the first squad, when training ended, came to us and said this player has to play with us.” Just days after that practice session, Diomandé was called into the squad to play none other than Real Madrid in the league. In the 85th minute, the young winger made his professional debut as a late substitute. Although his team lost the match 3-2, his cameo was enough to prove he belonged at that level. “The first time he touched the ball, he dribbled to Federico Valverde as if he wasn’t a special player,” Ortega said. “He made an impressive match, and well, he helped us a lot at the end of that season. He played 10 matches and was the best, he was very impressive.” Suffering total heartbreak But in that same year where things were finally taking off, Diomandé experienced true heartbreak. While away from home, he received a message that his sister, Roxane, had died after her drink was spiked at a party. “Everything I do on a football pitch, it’s for you,” Diomandé recently wrote in an emotional open letter to his sister and biggest supporter. “I don’t even look at it like a game. I look at it like a stage. This is my chance to show the whole world what you saw in me. Every time I score, I’ll make sure everybody knows your name. I’ll make sure they don’t forget you.” Roxane was one of the people in his life who truly wanted the best for him. Her death became another motivational factor in Diomandé’s meteoric rise through the sport. On the pitch, the cat was out of the bag. Everyone could see what sort of talent the Ivorian winger was. Leganés tried to increase his release clause, but the bids were already coming in for him. Eventually, a deal was made with German club RB Leipzig and a clause put into the package that meant Leganés would get a cut from any future sale. At that point, the Spanish club was confident he would soon be snapped up by one of the game’s giants for mega money, so was happy to play the long game. “We knew what we had at home because we were watching him every training session. We knew that the player was special,” Ortega said. “He reminds me of (Barcelona and Spain superstar) Lamine Yamal because of the way he’s able to drive, you know, to make it look so easy. It’s because he makes it easy and it’s so natural.” One season excelling in Leipzig, as well as a brilliant showing at this summer’s World Cup, was enough to convince the top teams to start battling for his signature. Move to the Spanish capital Real Madrid, though, was not to be beaten and saw off several complications to finalize a deal. A lot of the issues revolved around who exactly represented Diomandé at different times of his career, with legal cases slowing down proceedings. Several people from his past saw the move to the 15-time Champions League winner as an opportunity to cash in on a player that they always saw as more of a commodity – sadly something which is all too common in soccer and sometimes leads to young players not fulfilling their true potential. But those who know Diomandé best told CNN Sports that it’s always been about the game for him, not the stuffy suits in boardrooms trying to squeeze out every penny. Given the money paid for him and the talent he has, it’s easy to forget the player is still only a teenager. Just three years ago he was playing youth soccer in the US; now, he’s a global star. Despite moving on from the DME Academy, Eason still maintains a relationship with his former pupil and attempts to help him navigate the often treacherous industry. Eason acknowledges that all the agents and representatives from his past could have easily derailed Diomandé’s career, but in the end, it was the Ivorian’s pure talent that rose above everything else. Joining Los Merengues will now pose the biggest test of his career. The scrutiny at the club is like no other, the media attention can be smothering and the level expected from fans is so high. The winger will be under the guidance of legendary manager José Mourinho, who is an ambassador of African talent (Didier Drogba, Samuel Eto’o, Mikel John Obi and Michael Essien among others) but who is as cutthroat as anyone. But Eason, who last spoke to Diomandé when he was in the US for the World Cup, said he doesn’t have any doubts the 19-year-old can rise to the challenge. “My passion for our relationship is making sure he’s just prepared as a young man to handle what is about to hit him,” Eason said. “The one thing that I don’t think a lot of people really notice is just how competitive he is. “I don’t know where his ceiling is. I’ve never seen him be overly challenged, so I’m excited to see him with Real. He might not be listed on paper as one of the top three players, but I have a feeling he’s going to work his way into that pretty quickly.”
paragraphs: Yan Diomandé is set to have an incredibly bright future. At just 19, the attacker has signed for arguably the world’s biggest soccer team in Real Madrid and will begin his debut season for Los Blancos as they face Espanyol on Saturday. The Spanish giant signed the Ivory Coast international on a seven-year deal this summer, for a reported fee of $144.3 million. That not only makes him the most expensive African player in history, but one of the biggest transfers in all of soccer. But while many wax lyrical about his rags-to-riches story – one that saw him hone his skills in the United States – his is also a story of heartbreak and a reminder of the traps that lie in wait for young stars who aspire to become professionals. Diomandé was born in the city of Abidjan in the Ivory Coast. It was a humble childhood but one grounded by the importance of family and friends. A passion for soccer was there from the start and a young Diomandé could be found running on dirt pitches in just a pair of white sandals. In a letter he recently wrote for The Player’s Tribune, Diomandé says he was nicknamed after Brazilian legend Roberto Carlos because of his ability to strike the ball so hard. He was only getting started, but people could already see the natural ability that the youngster believed would one day take him to the top. He started playing more seriously for a local team where he saw his aspirations grow. It wasn’t long before he was telling friends he’d be the next Cristiano Ronaldo. The pivotal moment in that becoming a reality came when he was just 15. After representing his country at an under-17 tournament in Ghana, he caught the attention of scouts from around the world. All of a sudden, he was a boy in demand. But as is the case for a lot of young talent in the soccer industry, the teenager quickly became a commodity. Agents, coaches and teams all wanted to represent him, to sign him, to have some say in his future. Moving to Florida Eventually, through a convoluted arrangement of partnerships which stretched from Africa to the United States, Diomandé was offered the chance to join the DME Academy in Daytona Beach, Florida. He was just 15 at the time, but the move was supposed to help him develop in a professional environment which would prepare him for a life playing in the top echelons of the game. In truth, though, it was also a way of hiding him away from other agencies and teams that were sniffing around the player. The idea was that he would stay in the US until he was old enough to sign a professional contract at 18, per FIFA guidelines. So, with just a suitcase and a dream, Diomandé left his home and family in Africa on a one-way journey to the US. Picking him up from the airport in Miami was DME Academy’s director of soccer Todd Eason, a man who would become a father figure for a boy being pulled in every which direction. “Because he only spoke French, our communication was very limited on our drive back from Miami, which was four hours away,” the now Miami FC General Manager told CNN Sports over the phone. “We just exchanged little messages on Google Translate to try to get to know each other. But I also had other French-speaking players on the team, so it was kind of let me just hurry back to campus, let me introduce him to others that speak the language and try to get him comfortable there.” At DME, a small team of players would train up to six times a week and balance that with their studies. It allowed Diomandé to learn English and get used to a very different way of life. He quickly formed bonds within the team and, despite staying relatively quiet, would come alive on the pitch. He surprised even Eason, who had only watched his video highlights until then. Diomandé was not just faster than everyone else, he was more intelligent on the ball and was already confident leading by example. “I assumed we just had another strong player, maybe a little sharper than some of the other players that we had,” he said. “But I think once he touched the pitch and started playing, it was like, ‘Wait a minute.’ “Once I saw him, it was like, ‘Man, this is a different level than what I have and this is going to be fun.’ “To watch Diomandé play, it was just different in every way. I was very excited to have that opportunity and for the boys around him to be able to play with him because it was a considerable difference from the others.” Finding a new family Under Eason’s tutelage, Diomandé continued to develop not only as a player but as a person. But being away from his family wasn’t easy, especially in an industry that sometimes treats young players as cash cows. Instead of speaking only about the Beautiful Game, Eason would talk to Diomandé about his mother, who suffers from long-term health issues, and genuinely cared about the person behind the player. “He always wanted to get to the point where he could provide for his family and get his mom into hospitals to treat her,” Eason said. “I don’t think he’s driven by winning the Champions League; that’s a bonus, but he just wants to be playing at the highest level to be able to provide for his family and his friends.” Diomandé’s time at DME Academy ended in 2024, but he had already been invited to trials at professional clubs around the world. For several reasons, each would end up unsuccessful until a familiar agency got back involved. Ever since Diomandé had impressed scouts in Africa, he was being closely tracked and guided by American sports organization Blue Crow, which had invested in several professional teams across Europe. One of those teams at the time was Club Deportivo Leganés, which played in Spain’s top division, La Liga, at the time. With a keen interest in the African market, the club was tipped off about Diomandé at an early age and followed his progress in the US, eventually signing him in November 2024. The move was managed by Blue Crow, which was keen to secure its financial interest in Diomandé amid all the rising interest. The teenager’s move to Spain initially saw him play in the Leganés academy, then the reserves and then quickly rise through the ranks to the first team. Turning professional The club’s general manager Martín Ortega still remembers watching Diomandé train for the first time with the senior squad. “He was the best,” Ortega told CNN Sports. “The first time he took the ball, it felt like you were watching something special. You know, it was something impressive, special, not common at all. “Even some of the players of the first squad, when training ended, came to us and said this player has to play with us.” Just days after that practice session, Diomandé was called into the squad to play none other than Real Madrid in the league. In the 85th minute, the young winger made his professional debut as a late substitute. Although his team lost the match 3-2, his cameo was enough to prove he belonged at that level. “The first time he touched the ball, he dribbled to Federico Valverde as if he wasn’t a special player,” Ortega said. “He made an impressive match, and well, he helped us a lot at the end of that season. He played 10 matches and was the best, he was very impressive.” Suffering total heartbreak But in that same year where things were finally taking off, Diomandé experienced true heartbreak. While away from home, he received a message that his sister, Roxane, had died after her drink was spiked at a party. “Everything I do on a football pitch, it’s for you,” Diomandé recently wrote in an emotional open letter to his sister and biggest supporter. “I don’t even look at it like a game. I look at it like a stage. This is my chance to show the whole world what you saw in me. Every time I score, I’ll make sure everybody knows your name. I’ll make sure they don’t forget you.” Roxane was one of the people in his life who truly wanted the best for him. Her death became another motivational factor in Diomandé’s meteoric rise through the sport. On the pitch, the cat was out of the bag. Everyone could see what sort of talent the Ivorian winger was. Leganés tried to increase his release clause, but the bids were already coming in for him. Eventually, a deal was made with German club RB Leipzig and a clause put into the package that meant Leganés would get a cut from any future sale. At that point, the Spanish club was confident he would soon be snapped up by one of the game’s giants for mega money, so was happy to play the long game. “We knew what we had at home because we were watching him every training session. We knew that the player was special,” Ortega said. “He reminds me of (Barcelona and Spain superstar) Lamine Yamal because of the way he’s able to drive, you know, to make it look so easy. It’s because he makes it easy and it’s so natural.” One season excelling in Leipzig, as well as a brilliant showing at this summer’s World Cup, was enough to convince the top teams to start battling for his signature. Move to the Spanish capital Real Madrid, though, was not to be beaten and saw off several complications to finalize a deal. A lot of the issues revolved around who exactly represented Diomandé at different times of his career, with legal cases slowing down proceedings. Several people from his past saw the move to the 15-time Champions League winner as an opportunity to cash in on a player that they always saw as more of a commodity – sadly something which is all too common in soccer and sometimes leads to young players not fulfilling their true potential. But those who know Diomandé best told CNN Sports that it’s always been about the game for him, not the stuffy suits in boardrooms trying to squeeze out every penny. Given the money paid for him and the talent he has, it’s easy to forget the player is still only a teenager. Just three years ago he was playing youth soccer in the US; now, he’s a global star. Despite moving on from the DME Academy, Eason still maintains a relationship with his former pupil and attempts to help him navigate the often treacherous industry. Eason acknowledges that all the agents and representatives from his past could have easily derailed Diomandé’s career, but in the end, it was the Ivorian’s pure talent that rose above everything else. Joining Los Merengues will now pose the biggest test of his career. The scrutiny at the club is like no other, the media attention can be smothering and the level expected from fans is so high. The winger will be under the guidance of legendary manager José Mourinho, who is an ambassador of African talent (Didier Drogba, Samuel Eto’o, Mikel John Obi and Michael Essien among others) but who is as cutthroat as anyone. But Eason, who last spoke to Diomandé when he was in the US for the World Cup, said he doesn’t have any doubts the 19-year-old can rise to the challenge. “My passion for our relationship is making sure he’s just prepared as a young man to handle what is about to hit him,” Eason said. “The one thing that I don’t think a lot of people really notice is just how competitive he is. “I don’t know where his ceiling is. I’ve never seen him be overly challenged, so I’m excited to see him with Real. He might not be listed on paper as one of the top three players, but I have a feeling he’s going to work his way into that pretty quickly.”

articles.title: CM Punk vs. Kevin Owens Preview and Prediction For WWE Championship Match on SmackDown
articles.summary: Kevin Owens vs. CM Punk is the shot in the arm WWE SmackDown needed to reinvigorate its main event scene.
articles.body:
Kevin Owens vs. CM Punk is the shot in the arm WWE SmackDown needed to reinvigorate its main event scene.

The blue brand has been a bit of a slog to watch since WrestleMania season. Cody Rhodes has been a remarkable champion over the last two years, but his storylines have mostly grown stale or overwrought.

Even his highly anticipated feud with Randy Orton wasn't enough to improve his current standing. Their latest interactions have been much better, without Pat McAfee involved to distract from their storied history together.

Conversely, Punk's jump to Friday nights has been a net positive for the brand. His long-awaited encounter with Rhodes at SummerSlam didn't quite live up to expectations, but the weekly segments were worth the price of admission.

Now, The Second City Saint must face an opponent from his past on his home turf, making for a must-see television matchup on SmackDown.

Owens' return from a 17-month hiatus was one of the highlights of SummerSlam weekend. More to the point, his victory at the two-night event set the stage for a match many have salivated over since Punk returned to WWE.

It's no secret that these two men don't like each other. Their brief backstage exchange in December 2023 was enough to leave us clamoring for more. They crossed paths again on Jan 31, 2025, but the gloves came off during their latest war of words.

Punk and Owens referenced their infamous 2006 confrontation in the Ring of Honor locker room and the T-shirt that sparked it. Even more, The Prizefighter took jabs at his performative grandstanding, proclivity for burning bridges, and the way he treated his friends.

Obviously, this could refer to Punk's highly publicized altercation with The Elite—Kenny Omega and The Young Bucks. However, you would have to be specific, as the Chicago native bristled because Owens is also friends with Colt Cabana and others.

This worked so well because it plays up what we know about Punk's time with All Elite Wrestling and what we don't know about lingering animosity his current colleagues may have toward him. That didn't feel like a typical wrestling promo.

Their tension was believable, and it made for the best segments of the year.

Yes, we've seen other heated rivalries where someone expressed how much they despise Punk. However, this one wasn't merely based on his first stint with WWE or the seven years he spent away from wrestling.

His feud with Owens feels deeply personal. Even more, the Canadian wrestler excels at breaking the fourth wall and exposing another side of the top protagonists. That's also what made his storyline with Rhodes so good back in 2024.

KO is also the perfect avatar for anyone with grievances about how Punk's post-WWE run went because he's not just a WWE guy. He's famously worked with indie promotions like PWG, CZW, and ROH, and he's a part of the same friend group that founded and inspired AEW.

That makes his barbs feel genuine. These aren't just scripted lines from someone with no connection to that part of the industry. His words are more impactful because, under different circumstances, Owens could've shared a locker room with The Elite.

Even if you believe Sami Zayn didn't get a fair shake as champion, that makes it so easy to root for his longtime friend. It's hard to imagine WWE would fully invest in a Punk heel turn in response to the online outrage over his latest world title win.

The undisputed champion is too popular right now to justify it. Still, his upcoming match in Toronto has allowed him to play a more antagonistic role against such a relatable underdog in his home country.

Expect Zayn to take matters into his own hands and get involved in this match. After all, Randy Orton instigated a brawl with Rhodes to close last week's episode, costing him a shot at the winner.

No matter how close Owens gets to his first world title win in 10 years, it's a safe bet that Zayn will interfere. It's plausible that the two could team up again to end Punk's reign, but we're betting he will actually play spoiler.

It makes much more sense for the champion to retain and keep this feud going. Owens and Zayn are also likely to remain in the mix for the upcoming men's Money in the Bank ladder match.

Considering his claims of conspiracies to keep him out of the title picture, Zayn has the most well-established motives to attain the briefcase. So, Punk is our pick to win, but he'll have an even bigger target ahead of the next premium live event.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: Umyla Hanley and Hugo Savala added to England performance squad by Brian McDermott
articles.summary: England head coach Brian McDermott has added Umyla Hanley and Hugo Savala to his performance squad; Savala was born in Australia but is eligible through his English-born mother; The Rugby League World Cup takes place this autumn in Australia
articles.body:
England head coach Brian McDermott has added Leigh Leopards centre Umyla Hanley and Sydney Roosters halfback Hugo Savala to his performance squad ahead of the Rugby League World Cup this autumn.

Hanley, who was named in the Super League Dream Team in 2025, has impressed for the Leopards since returning from injury in May scoring six tries and providing 10 try-assists with Leigh winning nine of the 12 games he has featured in.

Savala has earned plenty of plaudits from his performances in the NRL this season with his Roosters side sitting second. The 24-year-old has crossed for eight tries.

  • St Helens appoint Australia boss Kevin Walters as next head coach
  • Super League's Final Charge: Seven teams in contention
  • Get Sky Sports or stream contract-free on NOW
  • Choose the Sky Sports notifications you want

A product of the Roosters system, Savala was born in the Sydney suburb of Randwick and is eligible through his English-born mother.

McDermott said: "When we announced the 38 players originally selected for the England Performance Group we made it clear there was still plenty of opportunity for others to play their way into contention before the World Cup squad is announced.

"Umyla and Hugo have done just that with their excellent form for Leigh Leopards and Sydney Roosters.

"We are entering the most intensive and competitive phase of the season, and the opportunity remains for a player to force his way into the reckoning. It's all to play for as regards the last few regular fixtures and finals."

England Men will kick off their World Cup campaign in less than two months' time against Tonga on Saturday October 17 at HBF Park, Perth before facing France in Perth on October 24 and rounding out the Group Stage against Papua New Guinea at WIN Stadium in Wollongong on Friday October 30.

England Performance Programme Group:

Junior Nsemba, Ethan Havard, Luke Thompson, Sam Walters, Brad O'Neill, Jake Wardle, Harry Smith, Zach Eckersley (all Wigan Warriors), Kallum Watkins, Mikolaj Oledzki, Ash Handley, Jake Connor (all Leeds Rhinos), Ben Currie, Danny Walker, George Williams, Matty Ashton (all Warrington Wolves), Kai Pearce-Paul (Wests Tigers), Dean Hadley, Jez Litten, Mikey Lewis (all Hull KR), Morgan Smithies, Jayden Brailey (both Canberra Raiders), Victor Radley, Billy Smith, Hugo Salava (all Sydney Roosters), AJ Brimson (Gold Coast Titans), Jack Welsby, Alex Walmsley, Daryl Clark, Harry Robertson (all St Helens), Morgan Knowles, Herbie Farnworth (both Dolphins), Mike McMeeken, Caleb Hamlin-Uele, Jake Trueman, Tom Johnstone (all Wakefield), Max King (Canterbury Bulldogs), Ben Talty (Brisbane Broncos), Dominic Young (Newcastle Knights), Umyla Hanley (Leigh Leopards).

articles.title: How to Watch 2026 INDYCAR Freedom 250: Start Time, Date, TV Channel, Streaming, Schedule
articles.summary: Watch the 2026 INDYCAR Freedom 250 on Sunday, Aug. 23 at 1 p.m. ET on FOX and FOX One. See the weekend schedule, course and streaming details.
articles.body: The 2026 INDYCAR season heads to Washington, D.C., for the inaugural Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, D.C.. The race airs Sunday, Aug. 23 on FOX and FOX One, with practice and qualifying coverage beginning Saturday on FOX Sports networks. Marcus Ericsson enters the weekend after winning the Ontario Honda Dealers Indy at Markham on Aug. 16. Àlex Palou leads the championship standings by 133 points over Kyle Kirkwood with four races remaining. Here is how to watch the Freedom 250, including the start time, TV channel, streaming information and complete weekend schedule. How to Watch the 2026 INDYCAR Freedom 250 Expanded pre-race coverage begins at 11:30 a.m. ET on FOX and FOX One. The race broadcast begins at 1 p.m. ET, with the green flag scheduled for 1:13 p.m. ET. Broadcast times are subject to change. 2026 INDYCAR Freedom 250 Weekend Schedule All times Eastern. Saturday, Aug. 22 Sunday, Aug. 23 Where Is the 2026 INDYCAR Freedom 250? The Freedom 250 takes place on a temporary street circuit around the National Mall in Washington, D.C. The course runs along Pennsylvania Avenue and passes landmarks including the U.S. Capitol and Washington Monument. The seven-turn circuit is 1.7 miles long. The race is scheduled for 147 laps and approximately 250 miles. Is This the First INDYCAR Freedom 250? Yes. The 2026 Freedom 250 is the inaugural INDYCAR race on the Streets of Washington and the first automobile race held on the National Mall. There is no defending race winner. Who Is Leading the INDYCAR Championship? Palou enters Round 15 of the 18-race season with 542 points. Kirkwood is second with 409 points, followed by David Malukas with 405, Christian Lundgaard with 403 and Pato O'Ward with 385. Palou can clinch the championship in Washington only if his lead grows to at least 163 points after the race. Who Are the Freedom 250 Announcers? Will Buxton will call the Freedom 250 alongside analysts Townsend Bell and James Hinchcliffe. Kevin Lee, Georgia Henneberry, Jack Harvey and Jamie Little will report from pit road. Chris Myers will host the special pre-race coverage with Helio Castroneves and Danica Patrick beginning at 11:30 a.m. ET. Who Won the Most Recent INDYCAR Race? Marcus Ericsson won the Ontario Honda Dealers Indy at Markham on Aug. 16. Watch the full highlights from the most recent NTT INDYCAR SERIES race below. How Can I Stream the 2026 INDYCAR Freedom 250? Fans can stream the Freedom 250 and select practice, qualifying and warmup coverage live and watch three days free on FOX One. Follow the Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, D.C. on FOX Sports for race information and results.

articles.title: South Korea footballers urge safety after extreme heat statistics
articles.summary: South Korea professional football association urges stronger heat protections in face of rising temperatures.
articles.body:
South Korean professional footballers urged stronger protections against extreme heat ⁠after a survey by the Korea Pro-Footballers Association (KPFA) showed many players hit by dehydration, dizziness and temporary lapses in consciousness during competition.

It found 86.2% of respondents suffered significant physical strain while playing in the heat, among ⁠536 players from South Korea’s K League and WK League surveyed during a summer when pitch temperatures exceeded 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit).

Nearly two-thirds (64.7%) complained of dizziness during matches or training, while 56.6% had severe dehydration and 13% suffered lapses in consciousness.

“The fact that over 70 players experienced dizziness, dehydration, and even temporary loss of consciousness is a ‌glaring red flag,” KPFA President Lee Keun-ho, a former national team player, said in a statement.

The union called on the Korea Football Association (KFA), K League and WK League to introduce mandatory heat protocols, saying the current safeguards do not sufficiently protect players.

The KFA told the Reuters news agency that player health and safety remained its “absolute top priority” and that it fully acknowledged the concerns raised by the players’ union.

The governing body said it was taking steps to reduce heat-related risks, including adjusting match schedules and enforcing cooling-break protocols during ⁠games, while also noting some logistical challenges.

“While we face certain practical constraints, including ⁠stadium availability and tight scheduling limitations, KFA is continuously monitoring conditions to make every possible effort to prevent any heat-related incidents,” South Korea’s governing body said in a statement on Friday.

Almost half the respondents said they were dissatisfied with the current cooling-break system that usually ⁠gives players a break of just more than three minutes once temperatures reach a specified threshold.

Nearly 90% supported changes to existing match operations during extreme heat. More ⁠than half favoured later kickoff times, while others backed postponing or cancelling ⁠matches when heat advisories are in effect.

The union said women players often face additional challenges, with a number of matches scheduled during the hottest part of the day on artificial surfaces and at venues without adequate air-conditioned changing facilities.

“Playing under the scorching sun on artificial turf that ‌traps and radiates heat is essentially forcing athletes into a furnace,” KPFA Women’s President Ji So-yun said.

“Just as professional baseball proactively cancels games for the heat, football needs to stop mechanically following a rigid schedule and ‌actually ‌prioritise player health and safety.”

The KPFA said the findings should also prompt a broader discussion on South Korea’s football calendar, with many players supporting a switch to an autumn-spring schedule.

articles.title: ‘It’s all I do’: Inside the year-long grind of the man behind college football’s Bible
articles.summary: Phil Steele is stumped. A man who spits out information for a living, who can recite chapter and verse on the offensive line at UMass, has no answer to an innocuous ice breaker of a question.
articles.body: Phil Steele is stumped. A man who spits out information for a living, who can recite chapter and verse on the offensive line at UMass, has no answer to an innocuous ice breaker of a question. He hems and haws for a few seconds before he finally gives up, admitting that he not only doesn’t have a favorite TV show; he can’t really name any. “I check the weather. I watch the news first thing in the morning,” he tells CNN Sports. “If my daughter wants to watch a movie, I’ll watch a movie.” Because, of course, Phil Steele doesn’t have time to binge-watch some Netflix or Hulu nonsense. He’s too busy consuming his daily dose of pigskin. The author of the veritable college football Bible – the eponymous “College Football Preview” – Steele long ago ditched such banalities as hobbies and pastimes. He watches college football. He rewatches college football. He takes notes on college football. He talks to coaches about college football. He writes about college football. He edits what he’s written about college football. He publishes a magazine about college football. Every year for the past 32 years, this is his livelihood and his life, his devotion to his craft so singular that only last summer did he finally see Europe for the first time. In return, Steele has carved a unique and profitable niche in the oversaturated American sports landscape by providing the two things fans crave most: information about their teams and the chance to sound smart. His is one of the few publications where the tagline – The Book Experts Cannot Do Without – isn’t hyperbole. Reporters and athletic administrators are among his most devoted buyers and coaches happily take his calls each year. The magazine’s arrival each year evokes the same giddiness kids once experienced when the Sears catalog popped in the mailbox around Christmas time, largely because it delivers the same sort of promise. College football can’t be far away. ‘It’s my world’ In 1992, Steele bought a six-acre property from the former wrestling coach at Saint Edward’s High School. The coach intended to use the barn as a wrestling room for his players. Steele has turned it into his rec room. There’s a trampoline, bikes and a full basketball court. Every day, along with hopping on his Peloton and ensuring he reaches his 15,000-step allotment, the proud papa of pigskin prognostications … hoops. It’s about the only time Steele isn’t watching or thinking or writing about football. “College football,” he says, “is all I do. It’s my world.” He came by his passion for pigskin honestly, through the pure-eyed adoration of childhood. Born in Cleveland, he rooted for his NFL (Browns) and college (Ohio State) hometown heroes, ravenously devouring the daily newspaper for information on his teams. His devotion changed when his father, Henry, introduced him to parlay cards – the pencil and paper betting sheets where picking multiple winners meant a nice little payout. A self-avowed math guy – “Don’t ask me about art,” he says. “I can’t even draw a stick figure” – Steele loved the challenge of studying and picking the winners in exchange for a few bucks. By 10, he was picking a steady stream of winners and crafting power rankings for his own enjoyment. Steele tried college, but nothing academic suited him quite like his love for football. At 21, he decided to bet on himself, quite literally, starting his own handicapping service. As Steele nuanced his skills, the service begat a newsletter – “Power Sweep” – crafted after his parents took out a second mortgage so he could buy a print shop. The first seven years he hemorrhaged money, his picks not nearly good enough to earn him a salary. Steele slept in the print shop, unsure what to do next. And then in 1989, the same year his father died of cancer, Steele went 53-23, the roll continuing through the next season. His handicapping merited attention and newsletter sales, but Steele soon tired of tipping his own hand to the oddsmakers in Vegas. “My underdog pick would start as a seven-point underdog, but then I’d put the information out and they’d be a four-point favorite,” he tells CNN Sports. “My picks lost value.” By the mid 1990s, the magazine section of the local bookstores and pharmacies were stuffed with football preview issues. Street & Smith’s was the originator, printing its first preview yearbook in 1940, but as the sport exploded, so did the market. Sporting News, Athlon and Lindy’s all crafted similar mags. Steele perused them on the regular, looking to pad his newsletter. Instead, he felt like he had more than they offered. The first “Phil Steele College Football Preview” was born in 1994. With 195 pages printed on black-and-white newsprint, it looked more like a beefed-up Daily Racing Form than a slick publication. Steele mailed it out to radio stations across the country, hoping they’d make a mention on air. “I had no idea what I was getting into,” he says. “Pretty soon, people needed the magazine. We stopped giving it out for free.” The making of the college football Bible The most recent issue of the magazine is a robust 375 pages and includes the same dense two-page spread for the Texas-San Antonio Roadrunners as it does for the Texas Longhorns. Every single FBS team – all 138 – is covered. It is not, by any stretch, literature, nor does it follow any sort of editorial style. Capitalizations show up at their leisure (Offense, Defense and Forecast) and some sentences require translation – Baylor 3-2 ATS L/5 vs FCS/under hit 3 str., for example. For spacing purposes, Steele has removed the following words – left, at, by, went, had, in, the, to, for, and, then and got – and has crafted his own abbreviations. DNR, in Steele’s case, is far less dire; it merely means a player did not return. The author – though Steele has a staff of around 10, he writes every word in every single two-page spread on every single team – makes no apologies. This is not a publication meant to meander through; it exists to provide information. There is an entire page devoted to NCAA experience, with an explanation of his formula used to rank teams and a two-page spread to cover the results of every single bowl game for the last 10 years. On the team pages, there are paragraphs devoted to every position, forecasts for both sides of the ball, nuggets to help set the stage for each game, and the past five years’ results, complete with the line. Not to mention predictions for the country’s top individual units, surprise teams (last year, it was Oklahoma, which went from 6-7 to the playoff; this year, it’s Alabama) and most importantly, his preseason top 40 and conference orders of finish. “My goal is to be graded as the most accurate magazine,” Steele said. “And I should be. Nobody puts the time into it that I do.” He is not exaggerating. Steele is a man of routine and excess preparation. He wakes each morning at 5:45, hops on his Peloton and watches one of two things – either an old game on tape or a replay of SportsCenter. If it’s the latter, he condenses the show into minutes, skipping through anything that doesn’t have to do with college football. After that, he heads to his office. On a college football Saturday, he will arrive by 7 in the morning and by noon has his bank of TVs cued up, 12 games running simultaneously. He’ll do the same for the 4 p.m. kickoffs before heading home for the night games, where he cuts back. Steele only watches eight games at once then. He gets by on a steady diet of caffeine, his self-deprecating “see-food” diet (“If I see it, I eat it,” he says) and an obsessive addiction to college football. It is impossible to see every play of every game, but the downtime in between allows Steele to scan back and forth. He takes copious notes on what he sees, crafting notebooks full of information and also creates and tracks nine sets of power rankings on a computer spreadsheet that, to the untrained eye, looks like color-coded gibberish. To Steele, it makes perfect sense. The portal has made his work harder, not just in terms of gathering information but getting a handle on whether a roster will and won’t mesh, but if he has a pet peeve, it’s the revolving closet of uniforms. “Sometimes, it takes me until halfway through the first quarter to figure out who someone is,” he said. A year-long passion project When the games stop, Steele continues. During the course of the season, he has a service that provides every article written about every team and when there are no longer games to watch, he reads. He’s looking for trends and progressions at various positions, subtle shifts he might otherwise miss in his game watching. Some schools might generate only a handful of print; a team like Ohio State, on the other hand, produces its own anthology. In the spring, he starts calling around to coaches. As the magazine’s popularity grew, so, too, did Steele’s reputation. Conferences started to invite him to speak at their media days, where he earned introductions to the men who headed up the teams he wrote about. For this year’s issue, Steele spoke to 133 of the 138 teams featured. It all coalesces through three edits and iterations into the one-of-a-kind magazine that comes out in July. Or Steele thought it was one of a kind. This year, a customer called Steele’s office to complain about the smaller book he purchased online. “We don’t have a smaller book, for crying out loud,” Steele says. A quick search revealed the culprit: Four fakes for sale on Amazon. A furious Steele posted a lengthy buyer beware warning on both his website and X, apoplectic that someone would steal his name and minimize his life’s work. Told that imitation is the highest form of flattery, Steele guffaws. “Not in this case,” he says. “They put my name on an inferior product.” The irony is not lost on Steele that what began as a passion project has, in some ways, altered his passion. Though his daughter is a nursing student at Ohio State, Steele is no longer a Buckeye devotee. His definition of a favorite team is the underdog he picked higher than everyone else. And while he devours more college football than ever before, the kid who once watched wide-eyed at his heroes can no longer watch a game without a clinical, detached assessment. “I’ll be in the barn watching UL-Monroe against Georgia State and I’m thinking about next year’s magazine,” he says. “Like how does the offensive line look?” But it does get him thinking, back to the original icebreaker question. Steele does, he realizes, watch a little TV for entertainment. “I like to watch FCS football,” he says. “I have nothing on it. Don’t have to make a pick. I can just sit back and watch.”

articles.title: Jannik Sinner pulls out of US Open with knee injury
articles.summary: Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open with a knee injury, the world No. 1 announced on Friday.
articles.body: Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open with a knee injury, the world No. 1 announced on Friday. “Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year,” Sinner said in a post on X. “We have been back on court in Monte Carlo over the last couple of days and have realised that I still need more time to recover from my right knee issue. I’m obviously very sad and disappointed, as New York has a special place in my heart. I was very much looking forward to coming back and playing in the electric atmosphere in front of the great fans there.” The news comes a day after world No. 2 Carlos Alcaraz announced his return to the tennis court after missing the last four months with a wrist injury. The 25-year-old Italian star has not played since Wimbledon last month, where he won his fifth career grand slam singles title. He later missed the Masters 1000 events in Montreal and Cincinnati. It is unknown when Sinner suffered the injury, but this marks the first time he will miss a grand slam since making his debut in 2019. Sinner won the US Open in 2024 and was the runner-up last year, losing to Alcaraz. Alcaraz makes his return Even though tennis fans will miss the sight of Sinner at Arthur Ashe Stadium, another superstar will make his return. The 23-year-old Alcaraz, who missed Roland Garros and Wimbledon with a wrist injury, will be back to defend his title. “Here we go,” Alcaraz said Thursday, along with a photo of him in front of the US Open logo. The US Open is a special tournament for the Spaniard. In 2022, Alcaraz won his first grand slam title in New York at 19 years old, making him the youngest ever to hold the top spot in the ATP rankings. The US Open main draw runs from August 30 through September 13 in Flushing Meadows, New York, with the men’s and women’s singles draws being revealed on August 27. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Mikey Lewis: Hull KR coach Willie Peters explains decision to drop star half-back ahead of two-match ban
articles.summary: Willie Peters chose not to include Mikey Lewis in his squad for Saturday's match against Toulouse as Hull KR look to 'uphold standards'; round 24 of Super League continues on Friday August 21, live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Hull KR head coach Willie Peters said his decision to drop Mikey Lewis for Saturday's game against Toulouse ahead of his two-match ban is about upholding the "standards" of the club.

Lewis copped a two-game ban after a Grade C charge for 'dangerous contact' with Warrington Wolves' Ewan Irwin during their rearranged round two fixture on Tuesday.

Lewis' studs hit the ankle of Irwin as he kicked the ball. Irwin is now an injury worry for Sam Burgess' side and is undergoing scans.

articles.title: Argentina’s Paredes gets 10-game ban for World Cup final scuffle with Spain
articles.summary: Leandro Paredes banned for 10 games as FIFA suspends three Argentina players for World Cup final scuffle with Spain.
articles.body:
FIFA banned three Argentina players, including a 10-match suspension for midfielder Leandro Paredes, for striking Spain opponents moments after losing the World Cup final.

The ban for Paredes, who grabbed Spain’s Eric Garcia by the throat and pushed Gavi to the ground, ranks alongside the FIFA sanctions for Uruguay forward Luis Suarez in 2014 as among the most severe in World Cup history.
